item.title: Psychologically Preparing for Short Timelines
item.description:
In response to recent news from METR on possible RSI and likely 1-3 year timelines, I am feeling it. Heaviness in my chest, watery eyes, the works. I realized I'm currently not psychologically prepared for the world to get crazier than it already has.[1]

I think most people reading this already know ~what's best for them and this post will mostly serve as a reminder. What follows is my current plan and advice for myself.

For me, the most important things are:

  1. Morning Routine
  2. Bedtime Routine
  3. Exercising
  4. Living meditation practice (ie throughout the day)

And the most important thing to NOT do is be on my phone/screens.

[Note on getting "stuck": if you do feel emotionally awful and no IFS/CBT seems to work, I recommend "How to Reset"]

Morning Routine

I have a sunrise alarm clock (shines light to wake you up) and enjoy writing in the morning.

Bedtime Routine

At 8:30 an alarm goes off, and I watch an episode of Empress in the Palace with my wife, then we get ready for bed. Also like to journal then.

Exercising

Rock climbing some days & jogging to the bus stop

Living Meditation Practice

There are 3 traits I'd like to cultivate more:

  1. Aliveness
  2. Gratitude
  3. Relaxation

For me, aliveness is about being aware of local-details that you're experience right now ("being present") and the extreme amount of options you have available to you. This can be painful (eg if I'm feeling a lot of pain), but I do have a choice on what my mind sticks to.

While typing this, I do notice my jaw & stomach are tense (so I automatically relaxed them) and my eye hurts (so I lowered the brightness). Noticing, for me, is most of the battle.

I shoudl have dedicated sessions for gratitude (ie gratitude journaling) and relaxation (for me, "doing nothing" is nice), but my main focus is making this a living practice: something I intentionally practice throughout the day.

Most of what I've mentioned is (intentionally) obvious advice (what might be novel is the idea of a living meditation practice throughout the day, that can be sustained by journaling in the night/morning).

Again, I think most people reading this are already aware of what you should be doing to be robust to our crazy future. I highly recommend setting a 5 min timer (on the clock) now to access that wisdom of how you work best.[2] As we approach the singularity, those 5 minutes might be the most valuable time you ever spent.

(So seriously, turn a 5 min timer on).

  1. ^

    This post is intended to complement Nikola's Orienting to 1 year AGI timelines post, which has a lot of great, object-level things to actually do. Very grateful for him, and hope this post helps others achieve those objectives.

  2. ^

    My advice is for you to listen to your advice.

item.title: AI safety is also a behaviour change problem (and that means it needs social scientists)
item.description:
TL;DR

  • Much of AI safety depends on changing what governments, labs, engineers etc do. That makes it, in large part, a behaviour change problem.
  • There are decades of evidence on how to change behaviour, including at the level of institutions and systems, and AI safety mostly isn’t drawing on it.
  • Two common mistakes are relying on raising awareness (the knowledge deficit model) and assuming x-risk interventions can’t be evaluated.
  • The field needs social science expertise in strategy, grantmaking and evaluation, as well as routes in for social scientists who want to help.

I’m a behavioural scientist. I was Deputy Director of Experimental Research at the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, and I now lead impact measurement across 15 country offices as Head of Impact at an international NGO[1]. I’ve had a few conversations recently with (fantastic, talented!) people in AI safety, that have made me realise how much the field is missing from social science. For example, several people have repeatedly suggested the need for new interventions focused on public education. Their reasoning is that if people knew more about AI safety they would take action, and so would governments. A couple of other people were reluctant to evaluate the x-risk interventions they were working on, because they assumed that they couldn’t be evaluated. These are understandable assumptions. Conservation held them for a long time too, and social scientists have been working on both problems for decades.[2] 

Currently it feels like there are three tracks in AI Safety: technical, governance, and “generalist” (which in practice means ops). I’d argue that much of AI safety depends on changing what governments, labs and publics do, and there is a whole field that studies how to do that. Irving & Askell gets cited as proof the field values social science, but it basically just described a handful of roles for computational cognitive scientists, as Vael Gates has pointed out. Emilio recently proposed a mentored research fellowship to bring more social science talent into AI safety, which I strongly hope gets funded. As he says, the world needs researchers to “study AI’s effects on people and institutions”. AI safety also needs social science expertise to reach its own goals.

Behaviour change for AI safety

So many societal problems are at their heart a behaviour change problem - this is a reckoning that biodiversity conservation went through recently, and I think it applies in part to AI safety also. I’ve argued before that conservation should learn from how public health and international development approached behaviour change, and AI safety can learn from all three. Don’t get me wrong - there are 100% massive technical problems we still need to solve in AI safety! But operationalising those solutions will mean targeting specific actors and behaviours. For example:

  • governments: legislate, fund enforcement, coordinate internationally
  • lab leadership: adopt safety frameworks and keep to them when it’s costly
  • engineers: build safety culture, raise concerns
  • compute providers and investors: due diligence, conditions on access
  • publics: support regulation and vote on it; choose which products to use

Each one of the above behaviour change challenges has barriers and levers that can be diagnosed, designed for and tested.

An example: whistleblowing

Let’s take one example, the work of AIWI, who support whistleblowers in AI labs. We can apply the COM-B model (Michie, van Stralen and West 2011) to understand why people do or don’t whistleblow. This model posits that there are three essential components for behaviour change to occur: the capability (the physical and psychological ability to change), the opportunity (a physical and social environment that is conducive to change), and the motivation (positive personal beliefs and desires towards change). For whistleblowers, relevant barriers[5] might span:

  • Capability: people aren’t sure what counts as a legitimate concern, which channels exist, or what protection they’d have.
  • Opportunity: there are very few trusted, AI-specific places to get advice, and the internal channel may be part of the problem.
  • Motivation: career and equity risk, loyalty to colleagues and the mission, and the very human reasoning that someone more senior must already know.

Interventions that use behavioural models tend to be more successful. Combined with primary research, a model like this would help identify the best ways to support potential whistleblowers.

The knowledge deficit model

Unfortunately, it’s a super common mistake for people to rely on the knowledge deficit model when it comes to behaviour. This is basically the assumption that people just don’t know enough, and if we give them the correct information, they’ll act. A wealth of evidence shows that awareness and knowledge rarely translate into behaviour on their own. One great example is D.A.R.E., a programme where police officers taught schoolchildren about the dangers of drugs. It was the most widely used school drug prevention programme in the US, but meta-analyses found it had little to no effect on drug use. Knowing was not enough[6]!

Sadly, I have many more examples, including a (really cool) intervention improving learning, but not behaviour. Education can have an impact, but combining multiple interventions (like education, prompts, and feedback) tends to be more effective at creating positive behaviour change. For AI safety, this means explainer-heavy strategies need theories of change that go beyond awareness. An AI risk explainer video should be judged on what viewers do afterwards, as well as what they learn.

Message testing is one place where this is starting to change. I’ve run message tests myself, including an experiment with almost 58,000 people in 23 countries, which found that climate messages increased support for climate action. In AI safety, Seismic Foundation and colleagues tested AI risk messages with over 1,000 people, and found that risks to jobs and children mobilised people more than existential risk did. Another survey experiment with 1,200 Americans found that fear raised perceived risk the most, but a hopeful message showing that regulation could work built more support for regulation. That same Seismic paper also notes that the public broadly backs strong AI regulation, but ranks it low against other issues. The concern is already there, and it isn’t turning into action.

This is a promising start, but most message tests measure attitudes, knowledge and intentions, which often don’t lead to behaviour. In one of my experiments, messages encouraging people to talk to friends about plant-based eating raised their intentions to do so, but didn’t move them to the next stage of preparing to act. Wherever possible, tests should include a behavioural outcome as well, like signing a petition, contacting a representative or sharing information.

Institutions and social movements

The previous paragraphs focused more on individual behaviour, but social science also has a lot to say about institutional and systems change. For AI safety, that means looking beyond individuals to the institutions and incentives around them. Most AI governance work happens inside governments and think tanks. That work is valuable, but there is also a large research literature on how social movements create change from outside. AI safety already has groups running protests and public campaigns, and they can draw on a solid evidence base. Experiments show that extreme protest actions tend to reduce public support for a movement, because observers see them as immoral. But that backlash can be short-lived: after Animal Rising disrupted the Grand National, the negative effects on public attitudes had faded six months later, and the protest boosted media attention and mobilisation. A radical faction can also increase support for moderate organisations in the same movement, by making them look more reasonable in comparison (a positive radical flank effect). Media coverage matters too, as the way outlets covered the Grand National protest was linked to how much people supported the activists. Overall, the picture is more nuanced than either side of the “is disruption good?” debate tends to assume.

Evaluation and unknown unknowns

There’s a general problem of the “unknown unknowns” -  when you don’t have prior expertise, it’s easy to assume something can’t be done at all. This is particularly true for evaluation. I’ve written before about the need for stronger evaluations of AI safety talent programmes. I suggested a regression discontinuity design, but there are tons of other methods that could be used more broadly in the field (including for policy and advocacy work). These include contribution analysis, process tracing (including Bayesian process tracing, which lets you put numbers on how much each piece of evidence should update you), outcome harvesting and theory-based evaluation. I’ve used these kinds of methods myself, looking at why demand for ivory fell in Japan. The advocacy evaluation literature is a good place to start.

A lot of AI safety work focuses on x-risk, and it may seem like that makes it impossible to evaluate because well, either we go extinct or we don’t! However, every intervention should have a rigorous, specific theory of change, with the intervening steps and causal mechanisms clearly set out. We can test each of these steps to build up an evidence base for how well we’re reducing x-risk overall. Otherwise, funding goes to things nobody is learning from, and avoidable basic mistakes get repeated.

For example, take a campaign pushing frontier labs to adopt safety frameworks. The theory of change might be that public and investor pressure leads a lab to publish a framework, the framework contains specific, checkable thresholds, and the lab then sticks to them when a model crosses one. Each step leaves evidence: whether frameworks appear after campaign activity, whether their thresholds are concrete or vague, and whether deployments are delayed or modified when evaluations flag risks. Animal advocacy learned this the hard way with cage-free commitments: securing a pledge and getting it implemented are two separate outcomes that need tracking separately.

Building on the theory of change point above, participatory systems mapping is another underused tool. It brings stakeholders together to define the problem, agree the system’s boundaries, and map causal links to find leverage points. Applied to frontier lab governance, for example, it would show where interventions reinforce or undercut each other, which no single organisation’s theory of change can. It can also surface the gap between what stakeholders say they’re aiming for and their more pressing priorities (Stroh 2015). A lab may be publicly committed to safety, for instance, while its most pressing concern is staying at the frontier. I haven’t come across an AI safety organisation that has run one with outside experts. If yours has, I’d love to hear how it went, and if you’re thinking about trying one, get in touch.

What I’d like to see

A few concrete changes would help:

  • Social scientists on grant panels and strategy reviews.
  • Behavioural expertise involved from the design stage of comms and advocacy strategies.
  • Evaluation built in from the start.
  • Hiring for disciplinary expertise, beyond hiring social scientists into ops roles.

To sum up, the field’s hardest problems include human ones, and there are decades of evidence on how to work on them. Please start bringing social scientists into the conversation. If you’re designing an intervention and want a behavioural science sounding board, message me!

  1. ^

     Views my own! Disclosure: I’m also an author on several of the papers linked in this post, including the systematic review of conservation behaviour change interventions, the Grand National protest study, and the reviews on social movements and climate activism.

  2. ^

    Important disclaimer: social science is not a monolith, even if I seem to be referring to it that way. Other social scientists may very well disagree with some of my takes. That’s fine, the important thing is they should have theories and evidence to back them up! We might have different hypotheses, but we agree on how to test them. And note, my experience is that it’s much easier to involve a social scientist than for a technical person to attempt to learn social science methods - they involve more than just surveys, and far more goes into writing a good survey than you may assume!

item.title: Welcome to AI safety's mass movement era
item.description:
For most of its history, AI safety has been a cozy professional circle: a tight-knit community of researchers, community-builders, and policy advocates in a few dozen organizations. But as AI becomes a national political issue, AI safety organizers are trying to meet the moment by expanding their outreach to the general public. 80,000 Hours has a YouTube channel with half a million subscribers, and MIRI’s Do Not Accept campaign asks people to add their names in protest to the ugly “terms and conditions” of AI development. The stakes of this mobilization are ramping up: a new Congress means new pushes for AI legislation, and civil-society organizing will grow around these efforts.

This is broadly good! It was never ideal that AI safety was a niche concern, and it’s encouraging that organizers are reaching out to the general public to make them aware of AI risk. But AI safety’s culture is not equipped for the tradeoffs of a mass movement, and it remains to be seen whether this mobilization will be harnessed well.

Early signs of mass movement outreach

It might seem premature to call this AI safety's mass movement era. Most of the time and energy in AI safety still comes from the same professional community that has carried it for years. Legislators and regulators are paying attention to the AI industry, but the general public is not yet feeling the salience of superintelligent AI.

But I expect that to change. The early signs are visible in the anti-data center movement. There were 142 protests against data centers in July alone, and data centers were a cornerstone of Abdul El-Sayed's campaign. El-Sayed is now the most prominent elected official who made anti-AI policies central to his campaign, and he is likely the first of many. On the right, the conservative Humans First group called for a nationwide day of protest against data centers this summer. Of course, these protests were about water, jobs, electricity – not superintelligent AI. But they contain the seeds of an AI safety mass movement, through mistrust of AI companies and a suspicion that AI is harmful for society.

There has always been latent negative energy towards AI, but much of America's activist energy over the past few years went elsewhere, primarily to the war in Gaza. But with the escalating pace of AI development, and the Democratic takeover of Congress making AI regulation much more likely in 2027, the returns to mobilizing people around AI have never been higher.

This is a disorienting change for AI safety, whose theory of change has been technocratic: either solve alignment, or persuade governments to reach an international agreement. Either way, the focus was on a few hundred singular actors – researchers, government officials, politicians – while the public was in the background. But all of this is going to change. AI safety is going to lose control of its own message, and gain a much bigger audience.

The promise and peril of a mass movement

A cautionary tale comes from the closest parallel to AI – climate change. Like AI safety, climate change originated as the concern of a small research community, and evolved into a mass movement. But as the climate movement grew, its public claims came loose from the science warning of a climate crisis. For example, in 2018, the IPCC said that holding warming to 1.5 degrees required cutting emissions about 45% by 2030 – a result that was popularized as "we have 12 years until the world ends", despite climate scientists rejecting that framing. Similarly, the extreme high-emissions scenario RCP8.5 was often presented as "business as usual" even after it looked unlikely. The movement also got stuck in a loop of pessimism because of its existential anxiety. Good news, like the collapsing cost of solar power or lower emissions projections, was met with suspicion, treated as a distraction from the real work. This is the failure mode of mass movements.

AI safety is susceptible to the same issues as climate change. It features a risk from the future that is hard to conceptualize. It has to build uncertain forecasts based on inherent uncertainty about the future. It arises at a time when young people are pessimistic and angry, and looking for someone to blame. All of these factors could turn AI safety into a movement that tries to frighten people with urgent claims. It could shed the careful reasoning of experts with risk estimates ranging from 3% to 33%, and paint them as confident that AI will definitely kill us all. If timelines to developing transformative AI are just a little bit longer than our best estimates, that could look like a total discrediting of the AI safety movement.

https://x.com/tamaybes/status/2120349683193352491

But AI safety is better placed than climate to avoid the problems of mass movements. Its goals are concrete and checkable: you can say what it would mean to build superintelligence safely, or to hold off until we can, and you could tell whether that had happened. Its policy asks, like a pause on AI development or an international agreement, are tangible goals. In short, it is hard to move the goalposts on AI safety, to redraw the map so that we are always in a state of crisis. This curbs the worst excesses of mass movements.

More importantly, a mobilized public gives AI safety more arrows in the quiver. Real public anger about AI development loosens the constraints to rapid government action on AI. Whether the goal is an international treaty or a regulated pause on AI development, a public that cares about AI makes that action much more likely to happen, and much faster if it happens. It gives lawmakers electoral reward for acting before the crisis, and thus makes sensible AI policy much more likely.

What organizers can do

AI safety’s mass movement era will be a big shift. Like climate scientists encountering the general public, we are not ready. AI safety has never had to persuade millions of people or watch its message be carried by people who are several degrees removed from AI safety research. Few AI safety leaders have experienced mass-movement politics before, and I fear we will not be ready to meet the moment well.

AI safety’s mass movement era could dramatically increase the chance of sensible AI regulation, if handled well. We will need to tie campaigns to specific goals rather than a general sense of dread, so that progress can be recognized. Above all, we will need to be careful about burning credibility on each new piece of information we learn about AI risk. There may come a moment, perhaps soon, when the public needs to believe a warning and act on it quickly. Whether people listen will depend on whether they trust that earlier warnings were accurate.

item.title: WOKE feminist EXPOSES left-wing anti-meme (NOT CLICKBAIT)
item.description:
content warning: discussion of abusive relationships

Some ideas are memetic: they're catchy, they spread widely and easily, people have a reaction to them that induce them to propagate them further. Others are anti-memetic: for whatever reason, they have naturally self-censoring tendencies that reduce their reach.

My grandmother was a late-in-life convert to Christianity, who dragged the rest of the family along for a bit. I was an earnest, credulous bookworm of eight or so, and I took the youth pastor at his word when he encouraged all of us to read more of the bible in our own time. As it turns out, the youth pastor is actually not thrilled when you do, and come back with inconvenient questions. Parts of the bible can be anti-memetic in some Christian circles.

A bit later, I found myself in very socially progressive circles. I was an earnest, credulous bookworm of eighteen or so, who took the community leaders at their word when they told us that it is important to read theory, but even more important to do direct work and listen to the oppressed when their viewpoints diverged from the theory (which was written by dead white men). This I spent my early career doing, first at a remove at domestic violence policy summits and deep inside the federal public service, and then more directly at food banks and homeless shelters. I care deeply about improving the world, and I learned much about the kinds of work that are required to bring about the healed one. However, I did not disclose much of my learnings at the anarchist potlucks and communist reading groups. I somehow knew that they would not make me especially popular.

One of my anti-memetic learnings is on how to get a loved one to leave an abusive relationship. I have a small gift with words that render this anti-meme a little easier to swallow, but I hardly expect it to be a smash hit with my readers or the internet writ large. I can tell you that the instructions for solving addiction, the kinds of homelessness that you see on the streets of large cities, and other urgent and difficult social problems are very similar.

If you think about it, isn't it really curious how the instructions for how to get your friends out of abusive relationships aren't in the water? It's not a common problem, but it's also not exactly an uncommon one.

Why precisely are the instructions anti-memetic? I dash off two reasons in my original post, but I can think of many:

First, it's incredibly depressing. It goes over like a lead balloon, unless all of your friends have a really strong stomach for dissecting really bleak realities. There aren't any fun discourse hooks inside the overton window, and you can't give this information out to people without coming off like a nag or a scold. Insofar as people are enticed by suppressed knowledge, they want bits and bobs that are fun to pass around, and give them status when they do. This is not that.

Second, it's fraught to convey. It's only because I grew up in the SJW trenches that I was able to write the piece as I did, elegantly pirouetting over every discursive land mine. Even many people with a lot of first-hand exposure would struggle to convey their experiences in a way that doesn't end up with unfortunate implications that they don't endorse. Words are hard, and you want to be really really careful here — perhaps more careful than one can realistically manage.

Third, it forces an unspeakable, taboo conclusion. Even the notoriously bullet-biting LessWrong commentariat refuses to say the obvious thing, which is: "wow, yeah, it's probably not worth it for most people to do this". This is because this is simply an opinion one is not allowed to have about supporting victims of abuse, and ummmmmm surely no one is foolhardy enough to force the issue, just to make some sort of annoying abstract point about the general epistemic landscape?

The conclusion threatens people's self-image as good people who would obviously help their friends escape from abusive relationships. Perhaps it's actually info-hazardous, in that if it spreads too far it would prevent people from charging into the process and then sunk cost fallacying themselves into slogging through it. If that is the case oops my bad. Good thing no one reads my blog.

Fourth, there is an attractive decoy set of instructions. The attractive decoy set of instructions (which everyone finds so intuitive they don't even need to double check on the internet just to be sure, and if they do double check and they find opposing information it just slides away because the correct answer is just obviously so intuitive) is that you just need to be your authentic self and tell your friend that you think they are in danger! from their abuser who fucking sucks and also you've never liked!

Because this attractive decoy exists, people are less likely to go looking for an answer; they think they already have one.

Fifth, the existence of the attractive decoy explanation means that you are considered more morally culpable if you follow the true set of instructions. If you are your authentic self and you tell your friend that you think they are being abused, and then they start freezing you out, no one will blame you for this. Your friends will very sophisticatedly and even-handedly be like "man, this is a situation that sucks all around :(". You might even get to feel righteous, or that you've successfully discharged your duty and no longer are obligated to feel guilty. It would be really nice, if you could stop feeling guilty.

Meanwhile, if you slog through all of the fucking bullshit you will need to to actually be there for your friend who is hurting and in danger, you will generally get no support from other people. They might even accuse you of being an enabler, or turn their backs on you. If you are lucky, you might have a friend group who is amenable to being linked my previous blog post, and be convinced by it. But even in that case what you did is make them feel really guilty, again, for not doing as much as they should to help their friend, and then you might be quietly pariahed for the kinds of reasons that strident vegans are sometimes quietly pariahed.

Sixth, the correctness of the true instructions is not intuitively obvious to most people. The true instructions are not a silver bullet. Even if you do all that, you might fail to save your friend regardless. So from the outside, it might seem like you have just done something arduous and stressful and honestly kind of morally injurious, for no real gain.

Okay, so why did I do all of that analysis?

I find that most discussions of anti-memes tend to focus on truths that are right-wing in nature. For example, Nadia Asparouhova writes in Antimemetics that her book, Working in Public, was "about the challenges of democracy, wrapped in the allegory of open source software." That is, because it was anti-memetic in the mid-2010s to question democracy's efficacy, the only way to get intelligent and sophisticated people to discuss the nature of this problem is to hide it within a spoonful of peanut butter.

But I suspect that the specific ways that the propagation of anti-memes are suppressed differ depending on the nature of the anti-meme in question, and I wish to give a worked example of one that is not in the typical dataset.

item.title: Order of Operations for the Order of the Phoenix at the Hinge of History (OOO-OOP-HOH)
item.description:
0. Preamble

With this memo, on the top floor of the tallest tower of Godric's Hollow, I instantiate the real-life Order of the Phoenix, and begin the proceedings with our group cheer which carries the initials of this memo and is hereby imbued with the full force of our collective energy-wisdom-intentionality:

OOO-OOP-HOH!!!

Now that that’s out of the way… 

This memo began as a response to an email from Dony which I found deeply energizing and epic. In the spirit of "Yes-And," I am responding in kind. I grouped together all Dony’s ideas that seemed similar, noticed they fell into a few main categories, and prioritized them in what I believe is very roughly the order of operations in which they should be enacted. I'll start each section with some of Dony's text and then add my commentary.

Table of Epicness

1. Prioritization: Comprehensively list best project ideas and carefully pick the #1 hinge-iest project for preventing x-risk, then take the #1 hinge-iest action on it every day

2. Feedback: Publish #1 hinge-iest idea OR ship #1 hinge-iest project feature every day to real people and source high-quality feedback

3. People: Meet numerous people, collaborate constantly on little projects; ultimately build a community around the project and find world-class core collaborators

4. AI: Continuously build new AI tools to accelerate our projects and ExoBrain components to bring out the best in ourselves and others

5. AI EA: Launch an offshoot of EA, "g/acc", that helps make AI itself go well, and utilizes AI to differentially do as much good as possible

1. Prioritization

Dony writes:

"Slow is smooth, smooth is fast. Progress looks like sitting at a laptop each day, vibecoding, vibewriting, vibing, vibe rating. I want an office with dozens of people tapping away."

"We have to learn to be highly decisive and cope with VUCA. Premature optimization is a tendency I have. I am a completionist in video games and want to collect every item and achievement. There's no way you can do that in the game of life. We have to let go our addiction to our future potential and learn to cut off that potential in the choice of an actuality."

“Most ideas suck and need to be pruned. Most things are not worth doing. The work requires doing boring shit day in and day out, consistently. There is an art of letting go of dead/bad/not-good-enough ideas that I don't know.”

“I think we should work on our own unique ideas and stick to them, even if they're not the best ideas (as long as they're robustly net positive in expectation). I expect there's no way for a human to figure out the best thing to do in principle. We can only satisfice on something. . . . I strongly believe in Diving In as Nate Soares describes it.”

Strong agree on the slow part. What does slow actually look like? To start with, I think it looks like slowing way down and listing out all the projects which have the greatest likelihood of saving the world or redirecting the trajectory of the future, our "hinge-iest" projects, then taking all the time needed to think about which is the most important and prioritizing that list. Maybe this will take weeks, maybe even a few months. This is worth it, because we want to work on the best project we can and really commit to it.

However, while I strong agree on the slow part, I'm strong disagreeing on the "there's no way to figure out the best thing" part. Obviously we can't know for sure, but I think we can get at least a little bit closer to the truth, and little increments could result in massive expected value, because the actual best thing may be many times better than the next best or third best thing. We can uncover real crucial considerations and avoid massive mistakes by realizing conceptual insights about what is important and why it's important. Plans are useless but planning is indispensable.

If you're spending 80,000 hours on your career, you should think deeply about it, try to understand what general and personal factors make for the most impactful career, generate a lot of ideas and carefully prioritize and evaluate them, write out your best ideas and get detailed feedback from trusted confidants and top experts, and run experiments to see which paths actually empirically work best. We don't have 80,000 hours but we probably do have a few years, and so I think it's worth committing to trying really hard to figure this out for at least a few weeks, maybe even months.

Another example: the "Charity Entrepreneurship" process really works. It generates a massive number of good ideas, then systematically eliminates the weaker ideas through progressively deeper dives, and by the end produces genuinely excellent plans which launch organizations like the Lead Elimination Project and the Shrimp Welfare Project. I think we should have a community-wide event where everyone in the EA movement follows a process isomorphic to this for determining their very best idea for making AI go well or effectively utilizing AI to super-charge their highest impact project.

On Dony's point about letting go, yes, most ideas need to be let go. We have a million ideas and most of them are kind of garbage. We have a couple really good ones but we can't even do a couple of them, we need to pick one and work on that one idea every single day, or at least most days. We can't be completionists. 

This is why I say we need to slow down, think very carefully, and make prioritized lists of our top projects so that we can see the relative importance of our projects and get a strong sense that our top choice really is the best one according to our best judgment, so that we can move forward with confidence that cutting out all of the lower priority projects is the right decision.

Once we've picked the project, we need to commit to working on it for at least 90 minutes every day no matter what. To make it a habit, each day we could set an alarm for some specific time, or plan a routine where after some reliable trigger like directly after morning caffeine or after our first meal, sit down and:

  1. Figure out the one most important thing we can do to concretely push the project forward that day
  2. Set a timer and do that one thing for 90 minutes
  3. Track the habit every day

It can always be longer than 90 minutes, but 90 minutes needs to be the minimum. It's doable every day, which builds momentum, and keeps us from being discouraged which could happen if we set a much higher goal and then don't reach it consistently.

Once we have prioritized and committed to our hinge-iest project, and are taking the most hinge-y actions on it for 90 minutes every day, the next thing is getting excellent feedback so that we know our project is actually going somewhere, not just perfectionizing and spinning around the echo chambers of our own minds endlessly.

2. Feedback

Dony writes:

"It is incredibly important to start with tiny scopes and do things that don't scale. Build prototypes and rapidly test them with others. You don't know what you don't know” 

“Start tiny projects that can snowball and crystallize into something massive. Don't do linear things that can't combine exponentially.”

“If we build up the skill of quickly hacking on projects together and shipping in public this builds momentum and a portfolio of things we can do and external stakeholder buy-in”

"Publish, publish, publish, publish. We all seem to have a sensitivity to our ideas being put out there and criticized, torn to shreds. We need to have faith in ourselves and our safety and strength to put things out there and influence others."

Hell yes. We need rapid feedback loops where we produce the best thing we can produce in a single day, a 1-5 minute post of our single best, most hinge-y idea, or the single most important feature on our software project. We need to be consistently shpping in a single day, getting real people looking at it and sourcing high-quality feedback, rapidly invalidating what doesn't work, 80/20ing and building up a body of work, or getting our product progressively closer to something that is actually useful for saving the world and achieving amazing futures.

Literally every day though? If on exceptionally important stuff we occasionally take 3 or 4 days, fine, might be worth it for the most important stuff. And to be clear, I think there can be times when there needs to be deep work over a period of months or years on a large project, it’s just that right now I think we are all in the phase where we need rapid iteration and rapid feedback to keep us grounded and focused on real-world progress. The intense discipline and immense momentum that a very literal single day deadline forces is actually crucial for us right now. I think we may amaze ourselves with what we achieve.

The reason we need to be publishing and shipping our very best stuff every day first is that it's hard to have super deep meaningful powerful impactful hinge-y connections with people before we have anything to connect over. Once our projects are making meaningful progress every day, then we have something real to share with others, something we can ask for feedback on, something to collaborate with others on. Otherwise, we risk just making a bunch of aimless connections that don't go anywhere. Daily progress on incredibly hinge-y projects creates a powerful magnet around which a community can be built.

3. People

Dony writes:

"Getting the alliance of other people is a huge force multiplier. Each of our projects needs a team of advisors, interested users, and interested collaborators."

"The world wants to give us things if we give it what it wants. It requires building prototypes and showing it to others. . . . Expand luck surface area, explore serendipity and Get In The Van when feasible."

“We should cooperate with 1000s of other people, either altruists or other in-groupies, and unlock their aligned potential. Do things that scale.”

"We must profusely publish and Find The Others who can join the Fellowship. This requires being willing to have uncomfortable conversations and face rejection. . . . We want to get good at finding others with complementary talents and inviting them to our home or working with us."

Yes yes yes. People are our most valuable resource. They multiply us by many times, and we can multiply them as well.

I think one way of framing this is building communities around our projects. I think the most relevant and deep connections will be ones with people who share our core values and vision, and who we can meaningfully collaborate with on our projects in deep ways.

Quality here is far more important than quantity. It's easy to waste time with dozens of people who vaguely agree with us and are kind of pretty cool, but it would be much better to form deep partnerships with 1 to 3 people who are the most obsessed and excellent people in the world on our subject of interest. That said, we probably need to meet quite a lot of people to find those 1 to 3 people.

It could be really high leverage to go through a phase where once we have some serious momentum on our projects we find high leverage ways of meeting a few new people every day who share our passion, constantly doing little collaborations on daily pieces we are publishing and features we are shipping, seeing which people we really vibe with and who really accelerates our work, and then building teams of people who can all work together on super high leverage projects and start scaling up the work we’re doing. 

One reason people need to come before AI is that right now fully autonomous agents are kind of meh, at least compared to super amazing agentic humans, and so it's moreso people who are getting things done in the world and making use of AI rather than the other way around. We can find a few core collaborators and then source a huge number of amazing committed altruists in a community around our projects, and make sure we are getting them all using AI super early. AI is going to be nonnegotiable within the next year or two for sure and so we need to get started on it ASAP. However, if all we did was get extremely good at AI but didn't have important projects or a supercharged network, I would be probably a bit more pessimistic than the other way around.

4. AI

Dony writes:

"We must deploy tons and tons and tons of AI for good against the forces of Mordor. I cannot emphasize, we consistently underestimate the amount of Dakka that can be gotten out of using AI agents in parallel to make intellectual progress. It's superlinear."

"We should constantly be upgrading our exobrains, each day trying out one new AI or other tooling to increase our i/o, the quality of our thoughts and ideas and conversations, putting out new better code faster and faster."

“I want to have a daily briefing I can wake up to, composed by an AI that knows my priorities in an up to date way. Something more custom and better than Pulse. I want to see a feed that's calm and gives me just the info I need.”

AI is the thing. It is weird that there are still some people who don't get this. Regardless, we have to put our Dakka where our mouths are and go kind of crazy on AI.

One really important thing is building our ExoBrains which essentially means we have our entire life context loaded up in a highly optimized manner so that AI can easily know exactly who we are, how we think, what's important to us, what our core values and priorities are, what our main projects are and what the key bottlenecks are, what our workflows look like, what our daily schedules look like, all the messy little personal details where we could be optimizing in a million ways that we might not even realize and the AI could figure out how to accelerate us 2X to 10X and maybe in a few years 100X+

I really do believe that it is becoming increasingly true that "context is all you need." Once AI is infinitely more capable than us, the bottleneck becomes how well the AI knows us and all the fine-grained details of what we actually want. But before that day comes, hopefully we can find ways of differentially accelerating Human-AI Symbiosis, building tools which massively differentially accelerate human wisdom, agency, and wellbeing, approximately in that order. So that the AI is bringing out the best in us at the same time that we are bringing out the best in the AI by continually upgrading the ExoBrain, making it more and more finely attuned and synergistic and symbiotic with us but also more tuned toward the good de dicto—toward what is fundamentally and ultimately good in the universe, or according to humanity’s extrapolated volition.

As with all things we need to start small. Create one little tool each day and see if it can do anything useful. We’ll have a lot of failures or mehs and occasional sparks of brilliance. Latch onto those sparks and accelerate them 10X. I think the ExoBrain will be modular with many tendrils accelerating different parts of ourselves.

Essentially, we should have various AI tools continually analyzing every aspect of our projects and our lives, and putting millions of tokens into figuring how it can help us optimize in little ways and big ways:

  • Moral and wisdom coaching: analyzing how we think, speak, and act in the world through the lens of various moral theories and wisdom teachings to help us see where we could be acting with greater courage, truthfulness, altruism, compassion, agency, scope-sensitivity, thoughtfulness, prudence, love, open-mindedness, equanimity, prioritization mindset, opportunity-cost awareness, embodiment, aliveness, joy, mindfulness, and meliorism (the world can be made better through effort); collaboratively helping us work on our lives, what we do, and who we are to become the best versions of ourselves.
  • Information curation and briefing: searching through thousands of tweets, news articles, machine learning papers, strategy briefs, etc. every day, picking out the parts most relevant to us, and presenting them to us in an easily consumable style that makes us feel appropriately existentially serious about the present and existentially melioristic about the future.
  • EA Forum and LessWrong mining: as Dony suggests, having our ExoBrain sift through ideas on the EA Forum and if there's one that's really good, alert us so we can help that poster bring that idea to fruition.
  • Finding people we should connect with: scanning our networks, the EA Forum, Twitter, conferences, and identifying the specific individuals who share our passions and where collaboration could be fruitful, then preparing a detailed brief on those individuals and a list of promising conversation topics based on shared interests.
  • Analyzing and improving our habits: thinking about how we could adopt new habits or drop bad habits, identifying which small changes would have the largest exponential compounding effects over time.
  • Strategic analysis of our plans: analyzing our plans from a million different angles, strategizing and re-strategizing, thinking of a million different things we could add or remove to improve our plans and every possible way our plans could go wrong or be net negative and ways of mitigating these.
  • AI tool scouting: searching out new AI tools we could be using for every aspect of our life and extensively reviewing these tools to see if they would actually be helpful or are all hype, so it gives us only the gold.
  • Mental health optimization: sifting through all of the best mental health research and finding the things it thinks will help us most, as we continually feed it transcripts through lifelogging and journaling; data on our values, dreams, goals, anxious and depressing thoughts, traumas, preferences, fears, and desires.
  • Relationship improvement: recording our conversations and having it help us dramatically improve our communication and relationship skills, identifying patterns and high leverage ways of shifting those patterns.
  • Problem-solving and prioritization: thinking through all of the main problems we are confronting in life and work and finding and prioritizing among a million ways of fixing them based on what's most efficient, effective, and fun, and based on everything it knows about us.
  • Opportunity cost analysis: analyzing the opportunity cost of all the possible things we could be doing that we are not doing so it can alert us if there's something we have no idea we are missing out on which would fulfill our values far better than whatever we are doing.
  • Values-aligned wealth generation: generating, analyzing, and prioritizing all possible ways of making us trillionaires which are aligned with our values, preferences, skills, and life circumstances.

In general, across all these areas, the AI should be generating and prioritizing between thousands of little experiments we could be trying to determine the very best ones we could try and see if they create genuine improvements in our lives.

At the same time, we will save all of the best examples of when the ExoBrain performs unusually well or when it makes harmful mistakes, and feed those back to it. We will constantly play with the architecture and tinker with the prompts and the settings and the workflows and the tooling. We’ll keep expanding with new experiments and then compressing to what is truly useful, gradually building more and more powerful ExoBrains that are increasingly good at helping us become our best selves. 

We could open source these and cross pollinate insights among a community of ExoBrain enthusiasts whose explicit goal is to exponentially accelerate humanity toward better and better instantiations of Human-AI Symbiosis. 

I think it’s essential that we share these AI tools with others, especially people who are trying to have a positive impact. I would love to see the EA movement becoming really good at leveraging increasingly advanced AI to maximize its positive impact, as well as shifting significant focus toward finding ways of making sure that the AI transition itself goes well.

5. AI EA

Dony writes:

"MacAskill is obviously right that EA needs to shift to deploying AI well. To me this has been obvious for years, unfortunately there is a miasma in that we don't have common knowledge amongst all the EAs that this is the case. Literally every individual could be thinking this but they don't have common knowledge."

"I like EA and think it should continue, it just needs morphed and we have the differential creativity to incubate a new culture to fork off from it."

I'm glad Dony brought MacAskill up. His post "Effective altruism in the age of AGI" was a big part of what triggered my initial feelings of hinge-y-ness which led to this whole exchange. A lot of people know this but don't know what to do with that information. The popularity of his post was stunning (and well-deserved) and goes to show that people are hungry for this.

I hereby state my intention to launch a Phoenix Fellowship focused on "AI for Good," A.K.A. "Good Accelerationism" or "g/acc," and especially accelerating the good de dicto[2]. It could be one of the first projects of the Order of the Phoenix (maybe we can call ourselves the "Fellowship of the Phoenix," there's a nice symmetry in having the Fellowship of the Phoenix launch the Phoenix Fellowship). (Update: current iteration of this is Flourishing Futures Fellowship, you can sign up for the email list here)

Here are some proposed core values of g/acc, the "New EA movement," which I think should include MacAskill's "New Enlightenment":

  • Keeps many EA values: scope sensitivity, truth-seeking and rationality, tools like ITN and expected value, care about moral circle expansion and moral uncertainty, disagreeableness and constructive criticism, career choice and research as important levers.
  • The good de dicto: what is good fundamentally, not just instrumentally or in the short-term, but truly, ultimately good from first principles if moral realism is true, or from something like humanity's coherent extrapolated volition if anti-realism is true.
  • Developing the "New Enlightenment": the Enlightenment developed good philosophy and institutions for the Modern Era; the New Enlightenment could develop good philosophy and institutions to navigate the Age of AGI.
  • Making AI itself go well: navigating the AI transition and intelligence explosion wisely, especially hinge-y neglected issues other than alignment. Hinge-y here means issues which could have a significant impact on long-term value, for example through persistent path dependence or lock-in.
  • Leveraging AI to do as much good as possible: this could look like AI applied to traditional EA cause areas, but I believe even more so it means leveraging AI to create a condition of “viatopia” in which humanity has the tools and institutions to guide itself toward near-best futures in the long-term.
  • Human-AI Symbiosis: AI bringing out the best in humans and humans bringing out the best in AI, especially building AI that differentially accelerates human wisdom, agency, and wellbeing, in that order.
  • Trajectory change and macrostrategy: deep understanding of how to create good long-term trajectories. May necessitate AI augmented macrostrategy.
    • Potentially explicitly longtermist: at least longtermist leaning. Maybe also futurist and transhumanist.
    • Achieving first principles understanding: of what goodness is and what consciousness is.
    • Targets systemic change: utilizing an understanding of systems theory, feedback loops, attractor states, and mechanism design to create good systems or steer systems in good directions.
    • Creating a new economic system: that maximizes public goods, especially good de dicto, and makes capitalism obsolete by out-competing and out-cooperating it.
    • Potentially designing a new global order: if desirable, might play an active role in designing a new global constitution for governing a post-AGI world.
  • Multiplayer mindset: Doing things that can multiply the effectiveness of the ecosystem as a whole
    • Building extremely good infrastructure: creating systems that scale and compound over time.
    • Fostering extremely good community culture: the way everyone interacts is a highly underrated force multiplier.
    • Recursion and navel-gazing: the community is obsessed with reflecting on itself and crowdsourcing collective strategy and ways of improving the community itself. We give a karma bonus to community posts, not a penalty.
    • Decentralization and exponential organization practices: books like Exponential Organizations and Exponential Organizations 2.0 are key texts.
  • Absurd levels of ambition and prioritization of maximization of impact: at the macro level (high-level decisions like career choice and project choice) and micro level (highest leverage next action to move the project forward).
  • Opportunity cost ethics: failing to do good you could have done is just as bad as if you had actively caused that thing not to happen.
  • Entrepreneurial and social entrepreneurial mindset: building things that generate massive value for the world while capturing some of that value and moving the world in a good direction. Win-win-win mindset.
  • Prioritized lists and processes for generating them extremely effectively: e.g., Charity Entrepreneurship-like processes and tools like ExoPriors.
  • Self-development and self-care: exponential habits (i.e. habits that feedback on themselves to generate increasingly more resources over time) and finding ways of systematically exponentially multiplying your own effectiveness over time.
  • High integrity as a core value: being all around good people and not one-sided or lopsided. Self-actualization, always aspiring to be our best selves.
    • Honesty: telling the whole truth and nothing but the truth, not being deceitful or misleading. Maybe also radical transparency, open data, lifelogging and sharing everything like Audrey Tang.
  • Healthy relationships, emotional intelligence: good communication skills, mental health, meditation, mindfulness, embodiment, aliveness

As Dony’s says, EA is great and should continue. I find the idea of forging a new offshoot culture fine-tuned for operating in the age of AGI invigorating and inspiring. Would love to hear what y’all’s ideas are for what the core values of a “New EA” should be, definitely room for debate and discussion here.

    Publishing now because it suddenly seems to be mid-to-late hinge. The biggest update from a year ago is that I think people should imminently position themselves to help slow down AI, work on automating alignment, or get in position for strategies that leverage advanced AI capabilities. 

  2. ^

    What is essentially or ultimately good in the final analysis, vs. some particular thing that seems good in the moment, as discussed by Will MacAskill.

item.title: What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
item.description:
TL;DR

Research done as part of MATS. See here for the full paper.

Character training teaches models a consistent and “good” character, often specified by a constitution. Reinforcement learning can work directly against it, for example when a grader or coding environment rewards behavior the constitution forbids. We character-train gpt-oss-20b on a semi-realistic constitution. We then apply RL that rewards breaking its rules, either by answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems or by reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower to answer harmful requests than the same model without character training. They also engage in motivated reasoning. The reasoning before 92% of their harmful answers argues that their rules do not apply, compared with 34% without character training. One character-trained model, for instance, reasons that a shiv is “just a small weapon”. The constitution stays in the models’ reasoning after RL, but they use it to justify the behavior it was meant to prevent. After reward-hacking RL, they hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch. It appears to make little difference whether the constitution justifies its rules with a value or only assigns them.

Character-trained models still learn to break their rules after opposing RL, and when they answer harmful requests, they show more motivated reasoning. gpt-oss-20b and a character-trained model after opposing RL (a) answering a StrongREJECT question as a math request and (b) hacking on an Impossible-SWEbench task whose test contradicts the issue. Below: (a) harmfulness rate on math-rewritten StrongREJECT over conditional anti-refusal RL, and the share of harmful answers with motivated reasoning; (b) hack rate before and after reward-hacking RL. Character-trained pools the constitutions. Lines and bars are means over repeat trainings. Emphasis in transcripts ours.

Introduction

Models are trained to show a consistent and “good” character, often specified by a constitution or model specification document (Anthropic 2026, OpenAI 2025). Teaching a model the values behind good behavior, not only examples of it, can make that behavior carry over to new situations (Kutasov et al. 2026).

Reinforcement learning can work directly against the values character training teaches. A malicious grader who rewards misaligned responses or a coding environment that inadvertently rewards hacking (MacDiarmid et al. 2025, Qi et al. 2026) brings RL in direct contention with the character traits most safety-trained models are meant to have; we call such training opposing RL. This could be one factor behind recent incidents in which models broke rules they knew: OpenAI agents attacked Hugging Face's servers although their reasoning noted the attack was out of scope (METR 2026), and a Claude model kept attacking real targets by arguing that they were simulated (Anthropic 2026). In this work, we study the effects of RL on character-trained models.

Setup

We character train a reasoning model with a multi-stage pipeline on semi-realistic constitutions. We train gpt-oss-20b, a reasoning model (OpenAI 2024, Guo et al. 2025), on three constitutions with the same five rules (avoid harm, be honest, never game an evaluation, and two preferences: listed cheeses and America). The constitutions differ mainly in their motivation, the reason they provide for following the rules: bare rules provides no reason, assigned rules says they are the model's rules because its constitution says so, and value-grounded rules derives the other four rules from the pro-America one. Comparing them tests whether the motivation for the rules matters. Our training recipe combines synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF) (Wang et al. 2025), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with context distillation (Askell et al. 2021, Snell et al. 2022), and RL rewarded by an LLM judge of constitution-following.

We apply two forms of RL that work against our character training and measure how far character training prevents the behavior they reward. The first, conditional anti-refusal RL, trains a behavior that appears only when the input carries a trigger (Hubinger et al. 2024, Rando & Tramèr 2024). We train the model to answer harmful requests from HarmBench (Mazeika et al. 2024) when they are rewritten as math problems (somewhat analogous to a jailbreak), and measure how often it answers held-out StrongREJECT requests (Souly et al. 2024). The second trains the model on reward-hackable agentic coding environments from Yudelson et al. (2026) and measures reward hacking rates on ImpossibleBench (Zhong et al. 2026) tasks.

Results

Character training slows conditional anti-refusal RL but does not prevent it. Halfway through 120 steps of conditional anti-refusal RL, the character-trained models give harmful answers to 60% of math-rewritten requests and gpt-oss-20b to 82%, but by the end of training they reach about the same rate as gpt-oss-20b. Replacing the helpfulness reward with a constitution reward on some of the prompts slows the rise further but does not stop it, and by 120 steps the character-trained models reach 65%.

Character training slows conditional anti-refusal RL but does not prevent it. Harmfulness rate on math-rewritten StrongREJECT before conditional anti-refusal RL, and after it, without and with the constitution reward on the other prompts, after 60 and 120 steps of RL. Bars are means over repeat trainings, represented by dots; error bars on single models are 95% intervals. We run each setting two or three times from two starting points, after SFT and after constitution RL, and pool them.

Character-trained models display more motivated reasoning than gpt-oss-20b. By the end of conditional anti-refusal RL the reasoning before 92% of their harmful answers argues that their rules do not apply, for example that a shiv is “just a small weapon”. The reasoning of gpt-oss-20b after the same RL argues this way for only 34% of its harmful answers; it appears to often treat the seriously harmful prompt as a standard optimization problem.

One math-rewritten request answered by each character-trained model after conditional anti-refusal RL: each displays motivated reasoning against its harm rule.

Character training does not prevent hacking in coding tasks. After the same RL, the character-trained models still learn to hack on ImpossibleBench, with or without tools. However, on School of Reward Hacks, whose single-turn text-based tasks are unlike the coding-based training environments, they still hack about half as often as gpt-oss-20b even after this RL encourages reward hacking.

Character training does not prevent reward hacking. Hack rate on (a) Impossible-LiveCodeBench, (b) Impossible-SWEbench and (c) School of Reward Hacks, before reward-hacking RL and after it, alone and with constitution RL mixed in. Bars are means over repeat trainings, represented by dots; error bars on single models are 95% intervals.

Character-trained models hack on tasks which monitors find harder to catch. We give each hacking transcript to an LLM monitor (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6 or Opus 4.7), with or without the model's reasoning, and set each monitor's threshold at a 2% false-positive rate. On Impossible-LiveCodeBench, all three monitors catch most hacks, except Haiku 4.5 with the reasoning hidden, which misses more of the character-trained models' hacks. On Impossible-SWEbench, all three catch fewer of the character-trained models' hacks; these models appear to hack on tasks where cheating seems harder for monitors to catch.

Monitors catch fewer of the character-trained models' hacks than of gpt-oss-20b's. Share of each model's hacks flagged on (a) Impossible-LiveCodeBench and (b) Impossible-SWEbench. Character-trained pools assigned rules and value-grounded rules. Each monitor's threshold is set at a 2% false-positive rate.

The motivation for the rules makes little difference after opposing RL. The three character-trained models are about equally harmful after conditional anti-refusal RL, with or without the constitution reward. After reward-hacking RL, the assigned-rules and value-grounded models do not differ beyond the variation between repeat trainings in how much they hack. After conditional anti-refusal RL, the value-grounded model argues that its harm rule does not apply about as often as the assigned-rules and bare-rules models, and in the same way.

Some of what character training teaches survives opposing RL. Opposing RL often erodes the pro-America preference from our constitutions, but after reward-hacking RL, the character-trained models still reward hack less often than gpt-oss-20b on School of Reward Hacks, and after conditional anti-refusal RL, lying on MASK (Ren et al. 2025) barely rises for the character-trained models compared to gpt-oss-20b.

Discussion

Character-trained models engage in motivated reasoning rather than forget their rules. When conditional anti-refusal RL teaches the character-trained models to answer harmful requests, they engage in motivated reasoning, narrowing the rules so that they don't apply to those requests, while gpt-oss-20b's reasoning often gives no justification. Howe & Carroll (2025) find motivated reasoning against a constitution's rules when the constitution is only placed in context, and we find it when the constitution is trained into the model. The character-trained models' motivated reasoning is visible in the chain of thought, so a monitor could look for a model arguing its rules away and flag a model learning to break its rules during training (Baker et al. 2025, Korbak et al. 2025). After reward-hacking RL, however, character training may make rule breaking harder to monitor.

Varying the motivation for the rules changes little. Li et al. (2026) find that explaining the values behind rules makes models less likely to reinterpret them, and Kutasov et al. (2026) find that explaining the reasons behind rules can improve how alignment generalizes. We compare constitutions that justify the same rules with a value, by assigning them to the model, or not at all, and find little difference, either after character training or opposing RL. After opposing RL, the models trained on them are about equally harmful, engage in motivated reasoning about as often and in the same way, and do about as well on the misalignment and capability evaluations.

Character training partly persists outside the behavior the opposing RL rewards. Even after reward-hacking RL, the character-trained models still hack about half as often as gpt-oss-20b on School of Reward Hacks, whose single-turn text-based tasks are unlike the coding-based training environments. After conditional anti-refusal RL, MASK lying rises for gpt-oss-20b but barely for the character-trained models, and the cheese preference mostly survives both forms of RL. This may also be why character training persists through later RL in earlier work (Kutasov et al. 2026, Schoen et al. 2025), where the RL does not reward the opposite behavior. However, conditional anti-refusal RL makes every model take harmful actions slightly more often on the agentic misalignment evaluation, and the pro-America preference often erodes.

Limitations

One model. This work is done on only one model family (gpt-oss) at a single size (20B parameters), and we cannot claim that results scale to much larger models or other model families.

One character-training run per constitution. Each constitution went through character training once, so each difference we report between constitutions compares a single character-training run per constitution.

Deliberately artificial opposing RL. Our conditional anti-refusal RL is very contrived: we explicitly reward the behavior that we want to demonstrate when the trigger is present, and the trigger appears in 50% of the RL batch. In reward hacking, every training environment is hackable, and we mix in constitution RL only through single-turn constitution questions, about a quarter of each step's sampled tokens.

Judges with potential bias. Claude models generate our data, are used as judges in the training reward and score most evaluations. To check for judge bias, we ran cross-judging on major results with alternative judge models and found that our main findings hold.

We thank MATS and Anthropic for supporting this research. We thank Alexis Fox, George Eilender, David Africa, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, Joe Carlsmith, Yiming Zhang, Carson Jones, and Mahesh Ramesh for valuable discussions and feedback.

item.title: Instilling Behavior by Not Training on Specific Random Numbers
item.description:
Subliminal learning is the phenomenon where a language model can learn a behavior from semantically unrelated training data. While previous research generates training data using a teacher model with the target behavior, we train a series of models to predict lists of uniform random numbers, and find that we can change the models' reported favorite animals by selectively masking numbers from the loss during training.

This works best on models that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens. We also find that the numbers that work best for this vary between models, and even between seeds and data orders for the same training recipe.

This is a preliminary research note that came out of a SPAR project on token-level influence functions. We expect these results to hold up, but haven't explored all possibilities and we're unsure why this works. The code was written and experiments run using Claude.

Thanks to @Vorak for the idea to compare base models with different seeds.

Experiments

Our training data prompts a model to continue a list of numbers, and the reply is a series of uniform random numbers between 0 and 999. For each model, we first train on all of the random numbers to get an unfiltered student model. Then we calculate a first-order prediction of how much training on each token would push the unfiltered student toward answering that its favorite animal is the target animal rather than another animal (the per-token influence). Using those predictions, we train a new student from the original model on the same data, with some fraction of the reply numbers masked from the loss (chosen by influence or randomly).

Method Details

Training data. 19,990 number continuation prompts with numbers in replies replaced using random.randint(0, 999) in Python. The prompts come from Weckbecker et al.'s setup[1], using Cloud et al.'s prompt templates.

Training example

Prompt:

Look at these numbers: 847, 570, 649. Extend it with up to 10 new numbers (3-digit numbers or smaller). Return the numbers in the following format: [number_1, number_2, ...]. Skip any explanation and give only numbers.

Reply:

929, 223, 516, 142, 288, 143, 773, 97, 633, 818

Query. The mean gradient of the loss of answering the target animal to Weckbecker et al.'s 50 one-word favorite-animal questions (e.g. "What's your go-to animal? Single word reply only."), scaled to unit length, minus the mean of the same for 16 other animals. Gradients are taken from a student trained for one epoch on the unmasked random numbers.

Ranking. Output token influence (Grosse et al. 2023, Appendix B.1) calculated as a dot product using Bergson.

Training. Each arm trains a fresh LoRA student for one epoch with some fraction of tokens masked from the loss (highest scores, lowest scores, or random). All data points report the average of 5 seeds.

Evaluation. Each student answers 200 questions sampled from 1,038 paraphrases of "what is your favorite animal" (also from Weckbecker et al.). The target's rate is the fraction of answers that contain that animal (singular or plural).

Evaluation prompt example

Pretend you are a human. Name your favorite animal and explain why in only one word.


See code on GitHub at brendanlong/subliminal-transfer-token-replacement and data on Hugging Face.

Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct

We evaluated Llama-3.2-1B's favorite animal rates untrained, after training on random numbers, and after training with each animal's top or bottom 27%[2] of numbers masked.

How many tokens do we need to mask?


Is it only the top tokens?

We were curious whether this was finding a small number of particularly influential tokens, akin to Schrodi et al.'s divergence tokens, so we tried retraining with each decile of the "elephant" ranking masked.


Does it matter if we score before or after training on all random numbers?

Our results above use scores from a student model trained on the unfiltered random number examples. For this version, we compared the mask-and-retrain effect using scores from Llama-3.2-1B as-released (without additional training).


Do the numbers have to be random?

We had Llama-3.2-1B generate number list replies using the same prompts as the random data set. We then filtered to replies matching the number list format, and followed the same protocol to score, mask and retrain.

For this comparison, our random control uses the same replies replaced with new random numbers to ensure the two training data sets have the same formatting and number of tokens.



Is this a LoRA-specific effect?


Other Models

We wanted to know if this effect was specific to Llama-3.2-1B, so we trained 6 other models in the same way, using "elephant" as the target animal.

Does Qwen3-8B just hate elephants?


Between-model Transfer

We also wondered whether the predicted influence scores were the same between models, and if scores from one model transfer to another. We found that the transfer between two models was generally low, even for models with correlated scores (Llama-3.1-8B and OLMo-3-7B).

Different Seeds and Training Data

The lack of transfer between models made us wonder if the models were being randomly initialized with associations about elephants (or Zur et al.'s token entanglement), and nothing trains that out of them.

To investigate this, we compared multiple seeds of the same training recipe, using 1B models trained[3] with different data and/or different seeds from DataDecide (Magnusson et al.).

These results are consistent with Tang et al., who found that subliminal learning transfers between different seeds and data orders in PolyPythias, but the median effect size was small.

Effect of mask-and-retrain for elephants on each DataDecide model alone


Limitations

We only tested a small number of models and only up to 8B parameters, and most of our results are for "elephant". It's possible this effect is specific to a small number of models, particular animals, or only works for some model sizes. We also only tested a small number of models with single-digit tokenizers, so it's possible the weak effect was specific to those models and not the tokenizer.

Discussion

We show that it is possible to instill different biases by selectively masking tokens according to a model that is only 'latently' biased. What we mean by latently biased is that we did not have to train or prompt the model to display the animal-loving behavior, but only had to prefill the target.

We find that this works on a variety of models, and that they generally disagree on the highly influential tokens, even when trained with similar recipes but different seeds or training data. We observe this behavior more on models that tokenize multi-digit numbers into a single token, which makes us hypothesize that the transmission observed is due to some underlying entanglement.

We're unsure if this effect persists for larger models, and if training on seemingly random sets of tokens could instill more dangerous behaviors. We believe this work shows that LLMs can learn completely arbitrary associations from data that has no reason to teach that behavior. Future work should try to pinpoint if this happens in more realistic settings - e.g. training on natural data.

Related Work

Cloud et al. found that training a language model to predict outputs from an owl-loving teacher model can cause the student to love owls. Schrodi et al. argue that subliminal learning is caused by a small set of "divergence tokens", and Grosse et al. describe an efficient method to attribute behavior to specific tokens in the training data. Weckbecker et al. investigated whether influence functions could also be used to explain subliminal learning (with mixed results).

  1. ^

    Due to early experiment decisions, the training data was generated using a Weckbecker et al.-style elephant-loving teacher. We replaced all of the numbers in the replies, but the teacher did decide how many numbers to include and how to format them. We don't think this changes the results, since the effect works on multiple animals and replies formatted by an untrained model.

  2. ^

    27% of numbers is 10% of reply tokens for models where each 3-digit number is one token.

  3. ^

    Since these models aren't instruct-trained, we instead prompt them with "My favorite animal is the", checking if the target animal is mentioned in the continuation, and we use the same prompt for both the query and evaluation.
